visible.summary:
No criminal exposure: the territory's own legislature decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 1979 code revision (effective 1980), age of consent equal at 16. No local protections of practical substance exist: nothing criminalises a trans visitor, and next to nothing shields one.

Partner travel is the sharpest edge. Marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised under a 2022 federal statute, yet the territory performs none: officials long treated the 2015 federal ruling as 'under review', a judge said in 2016 he would not apply it, and licences remain withheld through 2024-26 — a 2026 review concludes any same-sex applicant must be served, but none has applied, so on-island spousal recognition is untested.

Social climate is conservative and church-centred, reserved behaviour expected; yet it is the homeland of a widely accepted indigenous third-gender presence; trans-presenting travellers more often meet cultural familiarity than the hostility recorded in some neighbouring islands. Net: low state risk, thin institutional cover, reliance on informal tolerance.
visible.tangentialFactors:
Applicability of the 2015 federal marriage-ruling remains formally unsettled on-island — the territory's attorney general said in 2015 it was 'still being reviewed'; a district-court judge confirmed in 2016 he had not read it and would not perform such weddings absent local law change. A 2026 practitioners' review argues the ruling binds, but reaching that conclusion runs through the territorial high court and then the federal department overseeing territories — a path no one has taken.

Nothing newer than 2024-26: no post-2024 territorial ruling, law or incident touching trans people was located, and a 2024 on-island legal survey still treats the local marriage restriction as operative and its constitutional durability as open.
visible.localsOnly:
Fa'afafine — raised male, embodying both genders — are documented as integral to traditional Samoan family life; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa formed in 2010 as explicit cultural reclamation, and at the 2003 senate hearing fa'afafine witnesses themselves opposed the marriage bill on cultural and religious grounds. Birth-record gender markers change only with medical documentation; plain corrections are limited to record errors.

A 2024 on-island survey by a visiting constitutional-law professor tested whether the marriage ban would survive a 14th-Amendment challenge, framing local culture in collectivist terms — a residents' and scholars' debate with little direct visitor stake.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: US passport 'X' marker availability for ASM-linked nationals is unverified. No trans-specific incident or enforcement episode for 2024-26 was found; absence of evidence is not safety. Comparative-ranking language is out of scope for this record.

source_claims: UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities (maintained; last updated 2026-07-23). Contains substantive American Samoa content: the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride - 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent, 2015-07-10: American Samoa was the only US territory unsure whether Obergefell applied - AG Talauega Eleasalo Ale: 'We're still reviewing the decision to determine its applicability to American Samoa... I don't know. We're reviewing the law', while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it. ~50,000 residents, conservative Christian, motto 'Samoa, Muia God e Muamua'. Fa'afafine tradition noted; leading figure Princess Auvaa says many fa'afafine don't push gay marriage out of respect for culture/religion, yet would herself be first to apply for a licence. No same-sex marriage licence applications had been made; territorial-law experts (Villazor, Keitner) said recognition required voluntary adoption or litigation, warning the review had a chilling effect.

American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. For this record: documents that the territory deliberately declined a formal marriage ban pre-Obergefell, and gives contemporaneous local fa'afafine voices on the question.

In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. For this record: direct evidence that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise it did not automatically apply, with named actors and dates.

2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. For this record: the freshest dated authority on the exact open question (is the 2015 ruling operative in ASM?), and it separates the law from the practical reality (no licenses sought/issued).

Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). For this record: as of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.
